sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The note gives d^n as the size of a joint distribution without qualifying domain sizes.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Use the product of domain sizes, product_i d_i; d^n applies only when all n variables have the same domain size d.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: Conditional probability is worded as an event occurring after another event, which can imply temporal or causal order.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Define P(A|B) as probability of A under the condition/evidence B, with P(B)>0; conditioning need not mean B occurred earlier or caused A.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The notes identify events A and B as random variables.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Keep A and B as events; define random variables explicitly, such as X=number of heads or I=indicator that the first toss is heads.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: P(disease|symptom) is described as the probability that the disease causes the symptom.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: P(disease|symptom) is the posterior probability of disease given evidence. P(symptom|disease) is the likelihood associated with the symptom under the disease hypothesis.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The displayed total-probability derivation mixes union and addition notation and an unnecessary multiway-intersection subtraction.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: For a disjoint exhaustive partition {H_i}, state P(E)=sum_i P(E intersect H_i)=sum_i P(E|H_i)P(H_i).

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The rule argmax_h P(E|h)P(h) is titled Maximum Likelihood Hypothesis.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: This is maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. Maximum likelihood uses argmax_h P(E|h) and omits the prior.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: Independence is summarized only as P(x|y)=P(x).
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: State the condition for all values with positive conditioning probability, and give the equivalent factorization P(x,y)=P(x)P(y).

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: Naive Bayes is introduced as features being independent of each other without consistently retaining the class condition.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: The Naive Bayes assumption is conditional independence of features given the class: P(F_1,...,F_n|C)=product_j P(F_j|C).

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: A probabilistic finite-state pronunciation model is labeled an application of Naive Bayes.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Present it as a probabilistic finite-state or sequence model unless a class-conditioned feature factorization is explicitly established.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The advantages state that training only estimates mean and variance, which is specific to Gaussian Naive Bayes.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Gaussian Naive Bayes estimates class-conditional distribution parameters such as mean and variance; multinomial, Bernoulli, and categorical variants estimate different sufficient statistics.

sourceCorrectionLedger.sourceIssue: The references misspell George F. Luger as George Fluger and Stuart Russell as Russel.
sourceCorrectionLedger.correction: Use George F. Luger and Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig while preserving the stated editions and publication years.

Scenario: 
We toss a fair coin threesuccessive times. What is the probability of seeing more heads than tails coming up when the first toss is a head?
Q1: What is the sample space? 
Q2: What are the events and the probabilities of each event?
Q3: What are the random variables?
Q4: What is the probability distribution for “number of heads”?
Q5: What is the conditional probability and how can we compute it?

slides.speakerNotesText:
Q1:What is the sample space? 
S = {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT}
Q2: What are the events and the probabilities of each event?
A = {more heads than tails coming up} and B = {1st toss is a head}
P(A) = 4/8, P(B) = 4/8
Q3: What are the random variables?
Measurements of interest for any coin tossing event, e.g., A and B.
Q4: What is the probability distribution for “number of heads”?
Let X = “number of heads”. P(X=0)=1/8, P(X=1)=3/8,P(X=2)=3/8, P(X=3)=1/8. Show a table or draw a histogram of probabilities with respect to X.
Q5: What is the conditional probability and how can we compute it? 
P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = (3/8)/(4/8) = ¾
Or P(A|B) can be simply calculated by dividing the number of elements for A∩B by the number of elements for B. 
When the first toss is H.
The rest are HH, HT, TH, TT. So 3/4

You begin to search for possible explanations of the slowdown. Could it be road construction? Has there been an accident? Perhaps there are other possible explanations.After a few minutes you come across orange barrels you determine that the best explanation is roadconstruction. Similarly, if you would have seen flashing lights in the distance ahead, such as from a police vehicle or an ambulance, the best explanationgiven this evidence would be a traffic accident.

slides.title: Example using Bayes’ Theorem
slides.completeText: Example using Bayes’ TheoremScenario: Assume only three car dealers you will go since they all sell a1 model of car. Probability that you will go to each dealer is p(d1)=0.2, p(d2)=0.4, p(d3)=0.4. Once you are at a dealer, the probability to purchase a particular model of car a1 at d1,d2,and d3 is 0.2, 0.4, and 0.3, respectively. Question: You purchased an a1 model of car. What is the probability that you purchased it at the dealer d2? Answer: Given that you purchased an a1 model of car, you bought it from d2 out of three possible dealers. Basically you need to calculate p(d2|a1) based on the evidences you are likely to go to each dealer. p(d2|a1) = [p(a1|d2)p(d2)] / [p(a1|d1)p(d1)+p(a1|d2)p(d2)+p(a1|d3)p(d3)]	     = [(0.4)(0.4)]/[(0.2)(0.2)+(0.4)(0.4)+(0.4)(0.3) = 0.16/0.32 = 0.534
